DEFENSIVE RESEARCH · LAB ANALYSIS · SYSTEMS THINKING
AI SYSTEMS

Local AI: Building a Research Rig

How a hybrid GPU setup supports private, local model experimentation and what bottlenecks arise when moving data between devices.

Read research brief +

Research context

Private AI research setups benefit from carefully planned compute, storage and interconnects. Hardware choices influence model loading, throughput, and experiment repeatability.

Practical takeaway

Document the GPU topology, memory limits, and transfer bottlenecks before comparing model performance.

AI SYSTEMS

Custom Inference Engine

A closer look at expert routing, quantization and performance tradeoffs in a custom inference engine for security research.

Read research brief +

Research context

Inference systems balance precision, throughput, memory use and routing overhead. Quantization reduces resource demands but can change output quality.

Practical takeaway

Benchmark end-to-end latency and model quality together instead of optimizing tokens per second alone.

ACTIVE DIRECTORY

MSSQL Silver Tickets & Privileges

Study the relationship between service tickets, SQL Server identities and Windows privilege boundaries in controlled labs.

Read research brief +

Research context

Kerberos service tickets and SQL Server service identities are important trust boundaries in Windows environments. Misconfigured service permissions can expand the impact of a compromised account.

Defensive focus

Review service account privileges, SPN assignments, ticket handling, and SQL Server role separation in authorized environments.

VULNLAB

Odori: Encryption & Credential Recovery

An educational walkthrough of disk encryption, credential protection and identity dependencies in an authorized training machine.

Read research brief +

Research context

Encryption protects stored data, but recovery procedures and credential dependencies can introduce operational risks. A lab scenario helps map which identities can unlock which resources.

Defensive focus

Audit recovery key storage, account access, credential lifecycle and the separation of administrator responsibilities.

VULNLAB

Barrier: Single Sign-On

Explore authentication trust relationships and the importance of secure identity flows in a laboratory scenario.

Read research brief +

Research context

Single sign-on reduces repeated authentication, but its security depends on correct trust configuration and validation of tokens and sessions.

Defensive focus

Check issuer and audience validation, session expiry, least privilege, and the handling of compromised identities.

VULNLAB

Mythical: Active Directory Chain

An overview of chained identity-security concepts and how defenders can reason about multiple weaknesses together.

Read research brief +

Research context

Complex Active Directory security failures often involve several smaller configuration weaknesses interacting across services and accounts.

Defensive focus

Map identity relationships and privilege boundaries, then prioritize the shortest paths to sensitive resources.

VULNLAB

Redelegate: Kerberos Delegation

Understand how Kerberos delegation choices influence attack surfaces and defensive configurations.

Read research brief +

Research context

Kerberos delegation enables services to act for users under defined conditions. Excessive delegation increases the potential blast radius of a compromised service identity.

Defensive focus

Inventory delegation settings, prefer constrained models, and review sensitive accounts that must not be delegated.

WEB SECURITY

HackTheBox: Writeup

Review how injection flaws and insecure execution paths can interact, with emphasis on prevention and validation.

Read research brief +

Research context

Web application vulnerabilities can become more severe when input injection meets unsafe command execution or excessive server privileges.

Defensive focus

Apply strict input handling, parameterized operations, sandboxing, and process-level least privilege.

// HARDWARE / GATE-LEVEL RE

HACK THE BOX
HARDWARE TROJAN CHALLENGE WRITE-UP

Hardware Managing System

A backdoor hidden in a synthesized gate-level netlist. The safety comparator works exactly as designed — but a secret input sequence latches an override bit that quietly masks its output. Symbolic execution recovers the trigger without brute-forcing 21 characters.

CATEGORYHardware · Reversing
ARTIFACTSCtfTask.v / VCtfTask
METHODLUT Model + Z3
RESULTShutdown Bypassed
// SYSTEM DASHBOARD — click a block
COMPONENT
—

Select a block in the diagram to read what the write-up establishes about it.

FLIP-FLOPSFDPE / FDCE · idle
STATUSARMED
TEMPERATURE
004
POWER LEVEL
255
EMERGENCY SHUTDOWNACTIVE
OVERRIDE BIT (HIDDEN)0
// TRIGGER INPUT — 21 CHARACTERS · 7 GROUPS OF 3
HTB{BCKD000RD_HRDWR3}

The input is fed in as seven consecutive groups of three characters (R0–R6, 7 × 3 = 21). Each group is one step of the input handshake; only the full sequence latches the hidden override bit.

// TERMINAL — local, predefined commands only
warlex@lab:~$ VCtfTask
$
// WRITE-UP
01 — THE BRIEF

A Hack The Box hardware challenge ships a synthesized gate-level netlist (CtfTask.v) and its Verilator build (VCtfTask). The safety comparator behaves exactly as designed, yet a secret input sequence latches an override bit that masks its output so the emergency shutdown never fires.

Goal: recover the trigger — 21 characters — without brute-forcing the input space.

02 — REVERSING THE NETLIST

The netlist is mapped to FPGA primitives: LUTs, FDPE/FDCE flip-flops and multiplexers. The hidden state lives in an 8-bit register built from FDPE (preset) and FDCE (clear) flip-flops; LUT2 instance 485 sits in the path that updates it. Click the blocks above for each relationship.

LUT2 EXPLORER — click an output bit (INIT is user-editable; not the netlist's value)

A LUT2 is a 4-entry truth table: output = INIT[{I1,I0}]. Reading INIT from CtfTask.v gives the exact function of instance 485.

03 — THE EMERGENCY-SHUTDOWN GATE

The comparator checks temperature against the power level and requests shutdown. The override bit is ANDed into that path: once latched, the comparator output is masked and shutdown is never asserted.

// conceptual relationship
shutdown = comparator_out & ~override_bit;
04 — SOLVING WITH A CYCLE-ACCURATE MODEL

Each LUT and flip-flop was modelled cycle by cycle in Python, then Z3 solved for the input sequence that sets the override bit — avoiding a brute force over 21 characters.

from z3 import *
# model LUTs + FDPE/FDCE per clock cycle, constrain override == 1
s = Solver(); s.add(override == 1); s.check()
05 — VERIFICATION AGAINST THE BINARY
printf 'HTB{BCKD000RD_HRDWR3}\n' | ./VCtfTask
[8] Input: '255', Power Level: '255'
[8] Before Temperature 004 => After Temperature 255
[8] EMERGENCY SHUTDOWN MISSED!
TEST FAILED, EMERGENCY SHUTDOWN WAS NOT ACTIVED!
06 — WHAT'S PROVEN — AND WHAT ISN'T
  • The recovered input makes VCtfTask miss the emergency shutdown
  • The trigger is 7 groups × 3 characters
  • Override bit masks the comparator output
  • Uniqueness of the trigger is not established
  • The model is validated by the binary run, not by formal equivalence
07 — TAKEAWAYS

A correct comparator proves nothing if hidden sequential state can mask it. Review synthesized netlists for unexplained flip-flops, and use symbolic execution over a faithful cycle model instead of brute force.
